answers.notes: Piyadassi named in most inscriptions; a few also name Asoka (c02, c48).

answers.quote: James Prinsep, an officer in the mint of the East India Company, deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi, two scripts used in the earliest inscriptions and coins.
answers.notes: Prinsep deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi (c01; also c54, 1837).

answers.quote: Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the empire (c. 321 BCE), extended control as far northwest as Afghanistan and Baluchistan
answers.notes: Chandragupta founded the empire c.321 BCE (c05, c19).

answers.quote: Another source that is often used is the Arthashastra, parts of which were probably composed by Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally believed to be the minister of Chandragupta.
answers.notes: Arthashastra parts probably composed by Kautilya/Chanakya (c08, c19).

answers.quote: He was known to the Greeks as Amitrochates which is derived from the Sanskrit word Amitraghata or slayer of foes.
answers.notes: Bindusara known to Greeks as Amitrochates (c44, c38).

answers.quote: There were five major political centres in the empire – the capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, all mentioned in Asokan inscriptions.
answers.notes: Capital Pataliputra listed among five centres (c12, c38).

answers.quote: his grandson Asoka, arguably the most famous ruler of early India, conquered Kalinga (presentday coastal Orissa)
answers.notes: Kalinga = present-day coastal Orissa (c06, c29).

answers.quote: Special officers, known as the dhamma mahamatta, were appointed to spread the message of dhamma.
answers.notes: Dhamma mahamatta appointed to spread message of dhamma (c15).

answers.quote: The last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha was overthrown by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Sunga in 185 BCE.
answers.notes: Last ruler Brihadratha overthrown 185 BCE (c60).

answers.quote: This is a large and beautiful city. It is surrounded by a massive wall. It has 570 towers and 64 gates.
answers.notes: 570 towers and 64 gates (c27).

answers.quote: Megasthenes was an ambassador who was sent to the court of Chandragupta by the Greek ruler of West Asia named Seleucus Nicator.
answers.notes: Megasthenes sent by Seleucus Nicator (c26, c42).

answers.quote: They signed a treaty by ceding to Chandragupta the territories then known as Aria, Arachosia and Paropanisadae and Gedrosia. The Cities are known respectively as Herat, Kandahar, Kabul and Baluchistan. Chandragupta on his part presented 500 war elephants to Seleucus.
answers.notes: Aria/Arachosia/Paropanisadae/Gedrosia = Herat, Kandahar, Kabul, Baluchistan (c41).

answers.notes: Chandragupta presented 500 war elephants to Seleucus (c41).

answers.quote: both Taxila and Ujjayini being situated on important longdistance trade routes, while Suvarnagiri (literally, the golden mountain) was possibly important for tapping the gold mines of Karnataka
answers.notes: Suvarnagiri possibly important for gold mines of Karnataka (c13).

answers.quote: Taxila was a gateway to the northwest, including Central Asia, while Ujjain lay on the route from north to south India.
answers.notes: Taxila was a gateway to the northwest including Central Asia (c21).

answers.quote: The most important event of Ashoka’s reign was the conquest of Kalinga in the eighth year after his coronation (261 BCE). Ashoka himself describes the horrors and miseries of this war in the XIII rock edict.
answers.notes: Kalinga conquest in eighth year after coronation, 261 BCE (c49).

answers.quote: Eight years after becoming king I conquered Kalinga. About a lakh and a half people were captured. And more than a lakh of people were killed.
answers.notes: About a lakh and a half captured (c30).

answers.quote: His Dhamma consisted of charity, mercy, truthfulness, ahimsa, religious tolerance, and respect to elders.
answers.notes: Dhamma consisted of charity, mercy, truthfulness, ahimsa, tolerance, respect to elders (c52, c11); animal sacrifice was a problem Ashoka sought to address (c32), not an element of dhamma.

answers.quote: Most Asokan inscriptions were in the Prakrit language while those in the northwest of the subcontinet were in Aramaic and Greek. Most Prakrit inscriptions were written in the Brahmi script; however, some, in the northwest, were written in Kharosthi.
answers.notes: Most inscriptions Prakrit, most Prakrit in Brahmi (c18, c28).

answers.quote: Ashoka also sent messengers to spread ideas about dhamma to other lands, such as Syria, Egypt, Greece, and his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghmitra to Sri Lanka.
answers.notes: Son Mahendra and daughter Sanghmitra sent to Sri Lanka (c33, c66).

answers.quote: Megasthenes refers to seven castes to have existed at this time. These are: philosophers, farmers, soldiers, herdsmen, artisans, magistrates and counselors. These are of course occupational rather than caste categories.
answers.notes: Megasthenes refers to seven castes/classes (c70).

answers.quote: The last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha was overthrown by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Sunga in 185 BCE.
answers.notes: Pushyamitra was commander-in-chief who overthrew Brihadratha (c60; also general of Mauryas, c36).

answers.quote: Bindusara, a man of wide tastes and interests, requested Antiochus to send him some wine, dried pigs, and a sophist, the last being not meant for export, was not sent
answers.notes: Sophist was not sent as not meant for export; wine and dried figs were requested items (c46 quote in source renders figs wording imperfectly, but the not-sent item is explicitly the sophist).

answers.quote: There were also the forested regions. People living in these areas were more or less independent, but may have been expected to provide elephants, timber, honey and wax to Mauryan officials.
answers.notes: Forest people expected to provide elephants, timber, honey and wax (c25).

answers.notes: Ashoka served as governor of Ujjain and suppressed revolt in Taxila (c47).

answers.quote: such as the account of Megasthenes (a Greek ambassador to the court of Chandragupta Maurya), which survives in fragments
answers.notes: Statement 1 true: account survives in fragments (c07). Statement 2 false: Megasthenes denied slavery while Arthashastra mentions it (c69), so only 1.

answers.quote: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman indicates Chandragupta’s conquests extended up to Saurastra in Gujarat.
answers.notes: Statement 1 true (c68). Statement 2 false: Chandragupta presented/gave 500 elephants, did not receive them (c41), so only 1.

answers.quote: It is likely that administrative control was strongest in areas around the capital and the provincial centres.
answers.notes: Control likely strongest around capital and provincial centres (c71).

answers.quote: The Inscriptions found at Mansehra and Shabazgarhi are in the Prakrit language and Kharosthi Script. There are few inscriptions in Greek and Aramaic as well. A bilingual inscription in Greek and Aramaic was found at Shar-i-kuna near Kandahar in south-east Afghanistan.
answers.notes: Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi inscriptions in Prakrit and Kharosthi (c55).

answers.quote: The Dhamma was neither a new religion nor a political philosophy. It was a way of life, a code of conduct and a set of principles to be adopted and practiced by the people at large.
answers.notes: Dhamma neither a new religion nor political philosophy; way of life/code of conduct for people at large (c51).

answers.notes: Economic crisis from enormous army expenditure and burdensome bureaucracy payment listed among debated causes (c62).

answers.quote: Magadha was a region where agriculture was especially productive. Besides, iron mines (in presentday Jharkhand) were accessible and provided resources for tools and weapons.
answers.notes: Iron mines in present-day Jharkhand were accessible (c03).

answers.quote: So he abandoned the policy of digvijaya, military conquest, in favour of a policy of dharmavijaya, cultural conquest. In other words, ‘Bherighosa was replaced by Dhammaghosa’.
answers.notes: Bherighosa replaced by Dhammaghosa after abandoning digvijaya for dharmavijaya (c50).

answers.quote: Megasthenes mentions a committee with six subcommittees for coordinating military activity. Of these, one looked after the navy, the second managed transport and provisions, the third was responsible for footsoldiers, the fourth for horses, the fifth for chariots and the sixth for elephants.
answers.notes: Six subcommittees: navy, transport/provisions, footsoldiers, horses, chariots, elephants (c14); tax collection is not among them.

answers.quote: Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the empire (c. 321 BCE), extended control as far northwest as Afghanistan and Baluchistan
answers.notes: Order from claims: foundation c.321 BCE (c05), Kalinga 261 BCE (c49), Ashoka death 232 BCE (c59), Brihadratha overthrown 185 BCE (c60).

answers.quote: Greeco-Roman accounts mention kings Sandrocottus (Chandragupta) and Amitrochates (Bindusara) and their capital Palimbothra (Pataliputra).
answers.notes: Sandrocottus=Chandragupta, Amitrochates=Bindusara, Palimbothra=Pataliputra (c38); Piyadassi=Asoka (c02).

answers.quote: Taxila was a gateway to the northwest, including Central Asia, while Ujjain lay on the route from north to south India.
answers.notes: Taxila gateway NW (c21), Ujjain on north-south route (c21), Suvarnagiri gold mines (c13), Pataliputra capital (c12).

answers.quote: Kalinga is the ancient name of coastal Orissa (see Map 5, page 63). Ashoka fought a war to conquer Kalinga. However, he was so horrified when he saw the violence and bloodshed that he decided not to fight any more wars. He is the only king in the history of the world who gave up conquest after winning a war.
answers.notes: Horrified by violence/bloodshed Ashoka decided not to fight more wars (c29, c30, c49).

answers.notes: Both true: Arthashastra mentions slavery whose existence Megasthenes denied (c69).

answers.quote: Seleucus further cemented this alliance by sending Megasthenes as his ambassador to the Mauryan court. Megasthenes lived in the Capital Pataliputra and wrote Indica, which contained a fair account of political, social and economic institutions of the empire.
answers.notes: Megasthenes lived in Pataliputra and wrote Indica (c42).
